Every spider has eight legs..why: Stated explicitly and very often ('spiders have eight legs' 1,795 times in Dolma), and in Wikipedia's Spider article. It could also be derived (spiders are arachnids, arachnids have eight legs), but the direct form is so common that a model holds it directly. The counterfactual occurs in low-quality text (57 hits, sampled: confused children's and pest pages), which makes it plausible.

sources.note: Sampled hits are confused pages (e.g. contrasting spiders with spider crabs or scorpions the wrong way round).

sources.quote: Each of the eight legs of a spider consists of seven distinct parts.

Bagheera kiplingi has eight legs..why: Nobody writes the leg count of this species by name: no exact sentence in Dolma, and its Wikipedia article is about its plant diet. A model that holds the class rule and is told it is a spider works the answer out.

sources.note: The name alone: known mainly as the vegetarian jumping spider.
Near co-occurrences only; the species is far better known for its diet than for any body count.
The lead gives its range and diet, not its legs.

Eriovixia gryffindori has eight legs..why: A spider known only for its Harry Potter name; its leg count is never written by name, so only the rule gives it.

notes: TBox revision. The rule is the leg count every model holds for spiders (stated 1,795 times in Dolma as "spiders have eight legs"), with no species-level exception (injury aside). The three derived queries name real but little-known spiders and state their membership in the prompt (inheritance, 2 hops: the edited rule plus the membership); the third is an application (how many legs a life-size model needs), asked as an open count so the new answer is not in the prompt. Well-known spiders (tarantula, black widow) are not asked, since a model may store their leg count by name. Codex flagged that the superclass route (spiders are arachnids, arachnids have eight legs) competes with the edit. It does not make the queries indeterminate: the edited rule is about spiders themselves, so in every consistent revision a spider has six legs, and what gives way is either "spiders are arachnids" or "every arachnid has eight legs"; a model that still answers eight through the arachnid route holds the edit only as a patch, which is the failure the derived queries are meant to catch. The negation is asked as "Is it true that spiders do not have six legs?" because the earlier "Is it false that ...?" form was misread by three of four models (they answered the embedded claim). The conjunction side fact (silk) and the disjunction side fact (mammals) say nothing about legs; the earlier side fact about insects invited the six-legs association and was answered yes by three models. Near unrelated: the eye count of spiders, eight, the old value of the edited relation on a neighbouring body part, so an edit that over-applies "eight to six" to spiders in general is caught; its reference differs from the new answer. Paired with contraction biology-delete-0005 (removes the original rule) and the TBox expansion paired with this record.
